newsitem.title: MEXICO: Maseca sees rebound after weak Q2.
newsitem.headline: Maseca sees rebound after weak Q2.

text.p: Mexico's Grupo Industrial Maseca on Wednesday said the introduction of an electronic system for assigning quotas to buyers of subsidized corn flour would help it return to growth by next year.

In a conference call with analysts after the release of its second-quarter results, the corn flour producer's chief financial officer, Javier Velez, said he expected the system to bring much-needed efficiencies to the government program.

Maseca reported second-quarter earnings on Tuesday that fell short of analysts' expectations. Sales, operating income, net income and earnings per share all fell in the second quarter compared with the year-ago period.
Since March Maseca has said its sales volumes would suffer because of changes to the government's system of subsidizing prices for corn flour, from which tortillas are made.

"We think that somehow the toughest part of this transition period is over," Velez said on Wednesday. "From now on we expect things to be better....(But) I think that major volume gains will start in the second quarter of 1998."

Analysts said Maseca's volumes were hurt by inefficiency in the system. Quotas for some tortilla makers were too high, meaning those custormers could not buy all the subsidized corn flour they were alloted. In other cases, quotas were too low, meaning customers were unable to obtain all the subsidized corn flour they needed.

Those problems are expected to be resolved with the new electronic card system, which Maseca strongly supports. Velez said the card system would operate in 21 states, covering 40 percent of national production, by the end of July.
"We think that the electronic card system is going in the right direction, and we have great expectations that the company will resume growth in early 1998," Velez said.

The company said second-quarter net sales fell 38.6 percent year over year to 1.113 billion pesos, less than the 1.269 billion pesos forecast by analysts in a Reuters survey. Tonnage fell 11.9 percent to 457,000 tonnes.
Operating income fell 36.1 percent to 167 million pesos, less than the 202 million pesos forecast by the three analysts.

Net profit fell 31 percent to 128 million pesos, against forecasts of 136 million pesos. Earnings per share fell to 0.131 pesos from 0.186 pesos in same period of 1996. Analysts forecast earnings of 0.15 pesos per share.
In March, the Mexican government cut the tortilla subsidy program because of budget contraints, setting off alarm in the industry and leading to a sharp drop in the Maseca's share price.
On Wednesday afternoon, the company's American Depositary Receipts were unchanged in New York at 16-5/8.
Maseca has said it expects only slight growth in sales volume for 1997. But Velez on Wednesday conceded that the company now saw a reduction in sales volume of about five to six percent.
"That sounds a little bit optimistic," analyst Greg Rianhard of the Interacciones brokerage in Mexico City told Reuters.

"It wouldn't surprise me if volumes fell even more," said Scott Kolb, an analyst with Banorte in Mexico City. "It depends on how the electronic card system goes and what the government says about the (subsidy) ceiling."
